items.proposedEnglishModelAnswer: Food first enters the digestive tract by ingestion. Mechanical actions and digestive enzymes break it into smaller, soluble molecules during digestion. Most digested nutrients are absorbed across the lining of the small intestine into blood or lymph. Circulation delivers them to cells, where they are assimilated into body materials or used for energy and other functions. Material that remains undigested is eventually expelled through egestion.

The alimentary canal transports food from the mouth through the oesophagus, stomach, intestines and rectum. Chewing and muscular mixing help mechanical digestion, while enzymes and other digestive secretions break large molecules into absorbable units. Peristalsis propels the contents along the tract. The small intestine has a large folded surface with villi that supports efficient nutrient absorption into blood and lymph. The large intestine absorbs much of the remaining water before waste leaves the body.
proposedIndependentMarkingPoints: Nutrient transport and large-intestine water uptake

items.proposedEnglishModelAnswer: During inhalation, the diaphragm contracts and flattens while the rib cage generally moves upward and outward. This increases chest volume, lowers air pressure in the lungs below atmospheric pressure and draws air inward. During quiet exhalation, these muscles relax, chest volume falls and air moves outward. At the alveoli, oxygen diffuses into blood because of a partial-pressure gradient, while carbon dioxide diffuses from blood into the air spaces. Blood transports oxygen mainly attached to haemoglobin and carries carbon dioxide back toward the lungs.
proposedIndependentMarkingPoints: Diaphragm and rib action during inhalation
Chest volume and pressure cause inflow
Oxygen and carbon dioxide diffusion at alveoli

items.proposedEnglishModelAnswer: In inhalation the diaphragm contracts and becomes flatter and the external intercostal muscles lift the ribs. The increased thoracic volume reduces pressure inside the lungs, so air flows inward. During normal passive exhalation the diaphragm and inspiratory muscles relax, the ribs return toward their resting position and the lungs recoil. Thoracic volume decreases and pressure rises relative to the atmosphere, driving air out. Thus the two phases differ in muscle activity, chest volume, pressure and direction of airflow.

Blood contains a liquid part called plasma and several types of formed elements. Plasma carries dissolved nutrients, hormones, salts, proteins and many waste products. Red blood cells contain haemoglobin, which transports most of the oxygen. White blood cells help protect the body by recognizing and responding to infection. Platelets, together with clotting proteins in plasma, help form blood clots that limit bleeding after damage to a vessel.

Deoxygenated blood from the body enters the right atrium through the venae cavae, then passes through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. The right ventricle pumps it through the pulmonary valve and pulmonary arteries to the lungs. Oxygenated blood returns through pulmonary veins to the left atrium and passes through the mitral valve into the left ventricle. The left ventricle drives blood through the aortic valve and aorta to the systemic circulation. Valves help maintain one-way blood flow through the heart.
proposedIndependentMarkingPoints: Tricuspid valve/right ventricle to pulmonary arteries
Aorta to body and one-way valves

items.proposedEnglishModelAnswer: Blood reaching the glomerulus is filtered under pressure, allowing water and small solutes to enter the nephron while most blood cells and large proteins remain in circulation. As filtrate moves through the tubules, useful glucose, amino acids, salts and much water are selectively reabsorbed into the blood. Additional substances, including certain ions and wastes, may be secreted from blood into the tubules. The nephron adjusts water and ion recovery according to the body’s needs. The remaining fluid becomes urine containing wastes and excess water or salts.

Urine begins as filtered fluid within nephrons of the kidneys. After reabsorption and secretion, the remaining urine flows through collecting ducts toward the renal pelvis. Each kidney sends urine down a ureter by muscular contractions. The urinary bladder stores the urine until an appropriate time for elimination. During urination, urine passes through the urethra to leave the body.

items.topicId: Neurons - The Units of Nervous System
items.proposedEnglishModelAnswer: A stimulus is detected by a receptor, such as a sensory ending in the skin. The receptor produces signals carried by a sensory neuron to the central nervous system. The spinal cord or brain processes the information, sometimes through interneurons, and selects a response. A motor neuron conducts a signal from the central nervous system to an effector. The effector, such as a muscle or gland, responds by contracting or secreting a substance.

Nervous coordination uses electrical impulses along neurons and chemical neurotransmitters at synapses, whereas endocrine coordination uses chemical hormones carried mainly in blood. Nerve signals follow defined neural pathways and usually act rapidly, often for a short time. Hormonal signals commonly develop more slowly and may last longer. Neural responses can target particular muscles or glands through their nerve connections; hormones reach many tissues but affect cells with the appropriate receptors. Both systems coordinate body functions and can work together.
proposedIndependentMarkingPoints: Specific innervation versus receptor-defined hormonal targets

items.proposedEnglishModelAnswer: Ordinary human body cells usually contain two sets of chromosomes, one from each parent. During meiosis, germ cells produce gametes with one set of chromosomes rather than two. A sperm and egg each contribute a haploid set when they fuse during fertilization. Their union produces a diploid zygote and restores the chromosome number typical of the species. Meiosis also reshuffles genetic information through segregation and recombination, contributing to differences among offspring.

items.topicId: Role of Hormones in Sexual Development
items.proposedEnglishModelAnswer: At puberty, signals from the hypothalamus and pituitary gland stimulate the reproductive organs through a hormonal feedback system. The testes produce testosterone, which supports sperm production and changes such as voice deepening and body-hair development. The ovaries produce oestrogens and progesterone, which help coordinate the menstrual cycle and changes such as breast development. Pituitary hormones including FSH and LH regulate gamete formation and reproductive hormone production. Feedback between these glands and target tissues helps adjust hormone levels throughout reproductive life.

Chromosomes are structures made from long DNA molecules associated with proteins. DNA stores hereditary information in the sequence of its nucleotide bases. A gene is a region of DNA whose information contributes to a functional product, such as a protein or RNA. Before cell division, DNA is copied so hereditary information can pass to new cells. During reproduction, chromosomes in sperm and egg carry genetic information from each parent to the offspring.

Consider a simple trait controlled by two alleles, A and a, where A is dominant. If two heterozygous parents, Aa and Aa, reproduce, each can make gametes carrying A or a. Combining these gametes gives the offspring genotypes AA, Aa, Aa and aa. Their expected genotype ratio is 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa. Under complete dominance, AA and Aa show the dominant phenotype while aa shows the recessive phenotype, producing an expected 3:1 phenotype ratio in a sufficiently large sample.

In a general biotechnology workflow, scientists first identify the gene associated with a useful trait or biological product. A suitable delivery system, such as a carrier DNA molecule, helps transfer that genetic information into a host organism. The host cells that contain the intended genetic information are identified and examined for the expected result. Under appropriate controlled conditions, some host cells express the gene and produce the relevant molecule or trait. The product or trait is then evaluated for quality, effectiveness and biosafety before any permitted application.
proposedIndependentMarkingPoints: Choose delivery or carrier system conceptually

items.proposedEnglishModelAnswer: Biotechnology is used in medicine, for example to produce certain therapeutic proteins, and in agriculture, for example to develop plants with useful characteristics. Medical production can improve access to a needed medicine, while agricultural applications may help protect crops or improve yield under particular conditions. Another application is diagnostic testing based on biological molecules, which can support disease detection. Potential benefits must be weighed against risks, including unexpected ecological effects, product safety and fair access. Careful testing, oversight and clear labeling or monitoring where required help manage those risks.

Pathogens such as certain bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites can enter a host through the respiratory system, contaminated food or water, damaged skin or other routes. They may multiply within the host or produce substances that damage tissues and disrupt normal functions. Symptoms arise from tissue damage and the body’s immune response. Transmission can occur through droplets, contaminated surfaces, food, water or vectors, depending on the pathogen. Handwashing, safe food and water, appropriate ventilation, vaccination when available and other route-specific public-health measures help reduce spread.

Innate immunity provides rapid, broadly acting defenses, including skin barriers, inflammatory responses and phagocytic cells. Adaptive immunity uses particular lymphocytes to recognize specific antigens and may involve antibodies or specialized cellular responses. After exposure, some adaptive immune cells remain as memory cells that respond more quickly on later encounters. Vaccination presents the immune system with a safe form or component of a pathogen, or instructions for making an antigen, so adaptive protection can develop. Vaccination greatly reduces the risk of certain infections or severe disease without requiring the person to experience the full disease.
proposedIndependentMarkingPoints: Lymphocytes and antibody or cellular actions
Vaccine-induced protective response without full disease

items.topicId: Theory of Evolution by Natural Selection
items.proposedEnglishModelAnswer: Individuals in a population show variation, some of which is inherited. Environmental pressures can make particular inherited traits more helpful for survival or reproduction than alternatives. Individuals with advantageous heritable traits may leave more surviving offspring on average, passing their alleles to later generations. Across many generations, the frequencies of those inherited variants can increase, although conditions can change. Natural selection therefore changes population characteristics over time rather than deliberately changing an individual because it needs to adapt.
proposedIndependentMarkingPoints: Population change across generations, not purposeful individual change

items.proposedEnglishModelAnswer: Fossils reveal organisms that lived at different times and can show changes in body form across geological history. Comparative anatomy can identify homologous structures that share underlying features despite serving different functions, suggesting shared ancestry. Similarities and differences in DNA and protein sequences provide another independent way to estimate evolutionary relationships. Biogeography and some developmental patterns also offer clues about how related organisms diversified. When these different lines of evidence support a consistent branching history, confidence in the proposed relationships increases.
proposedIndependentMarkingPoints: Independent lines supporting a shared ancestry hypothesis
